agents.name: Lomustine
agents.explanation: Lomustine is an oral nitrosourea chemotherapy that can reach the brain. It damages DNA and interferes with cell division. Its effects on healthy blood-forming cells can appear several weeks after the dose and can build up over successive cycles. This explains the long gap between doses and the need for continuing blood tests.
agents.watch: This is one dose on Day 1, not a daily medicine. If an extra dose is taken, get urgent advice even if you feel well. Keep blood tests after the dose and report fever, bruising, bleeding, new cough or breathlessness.
risks: Delayed and cumulative low blood counts
Rare second cancers and fertility effects

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.mechanism: Forms DNA links that disrupt cell division
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms chemical links within DNA, making it harder for cells to copy and repair their genetic material. It can damage tumour cells but also affect kidney function, hearing, nerves and blood-forming cells. Fluids, electrolyte checks and anti-sickness medicines are part of the treatment plan to reduce avoidable harm.
agents.watch: Report ringing or reduced hearing, numbness or weakness, reduced urine, persistent vomiting or difficulty drinking. Tell the team about fluid restrictions or heart and kidney conditions before hydration.
risks: Nausea and vomiting, including after the infusion day
Kidney injury and changes in salts such as magnesium
Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Fertility effects and harm to a pregnancy

agents.name: Vincristine
agents.mechanism: Disrupts the machinery used for cell division
agents.explanation: Vincristine interferes with structures that cells use when dividing. It can also affect nerves controlling sensation, strength and bowel movement. This explains why tingling, weakness and constipation need early review even if blood tests are satisfactory.
visual: Nerves and bowel may be affected
agents.watch: Report tingling, weakness, walking difficulty or constipation before the next dose. Tell staff immediately if the infusion site stings, burns or swells.
risks: Tissue injury if medicine leaks outside the vein

anatomy_note: Selected regimen-specific effects are anchored to the retained detailed body illustration. Brain symptoms may reflect the tumour, treatment or another medicine; effects may involve more than one area. This is not the complete side-effect list.
anatomy: Report new ringing or reduced hearing promptly. New seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty needs emergency help.
Soreness or ulcers can limit intake. Use gentle mouth care and ask for help before eating or drinking becomes difficult.
Counts can fall weeks after lomustine. Fever, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding needs urgent advice.
Report new cough or breathlessness. Keep the lung checks arranged; severe breathing difficulty needs emergency help.
Attend kidney and electrolyte checks. Follow your individual fluid plan; report reduced urine, swelling or difficulty drinking.
Use prescribed anti-sickness and bowel medicines. Severe pain, vomiting or no stool or wind needs urgent advice.

Discuss preservation and contraception before starting. Do not breastfeed during treatment; ask for written precautions.

day_groups.action: Confirm hearing, kidney, bowel and nerve symptoms before treatment.

day_groups.action: A held dose needs a new team decision; do not replace it yourself.

chronology_notes.title: A treatment record is not a prescription
chronology_notes.text: The team may delay, alter or stop a component after reviewing symptoms, blood tests, organ function and previous toxicity. Do not restart a held medicine or add a replacement dose yourself.

chronology_notes.title: Lomustine is one dose, not daily
chronology_notes.text: Only the authorised Day 1 dose belongs to this cycle. Do not take a further course before six weeks and a new team decision. Taking repeated daily doses can cause serious harm. If a dose is missed or vomited, contact the team or pharmacist before taking any more. If an extra dose is taken, seek urgent clinical advice straight away even if you feel well; do not wait for symptoms.

chronology_notes.title: Delayed marrow effects
chronology_notes.text: Current lomustine product information advises blood counts weekly for at least six weeks after a dose. Low counts may be delayed and cumulative, so keep checks even when you feel well or the next treatment is postponed.

administration_text: Take lomustine only once on the authorised Day 1. The pharmacist must confirm the total dose, capsule strengths, how to take it and anti-sickness timing. Do not open or crush capsules or take another dose to replace a missed or vomited one without advice. Cisplatin and vincristine are given into a vein. Day 1 includes fluids before and after cisplatin; later visits on Days 8 and 15 are for vincristine. The total visit is longer than the infusion itself.

support.title: Anti-sickness plan checked for interactions
support.text: Cisplatin has high emetic potential; lomustine adds oral moderate-to-high risk. Use the team’s prevention and rescue plan, including delayed nausea after Day 1. Aprepitant and some antifungals interact with vincristine, so the oncology pharmacist must select and check the plan; do not add medicines yourself.

support.title: Hydration and electrolytes
support.text: Cisplatin needs fluids before and after treatment and an individual electrolyte plan. Tell the team about fluid limits, swelling, heart or kidney conditions, vomiting and reduced urine. Follow your own home-drinking advice rather than a universal volume.

support.title: Prevent constipation and monitor nerves
support.text: NCCP recommends preventive laxatives with vincristine. Report constipation, new tingling, weakness, balance or hand-function changes before each visit. Severe abdominal pain, vomiting or inability to pass stool or wind needs urgent assessment.

support.title: Medicines, infection prevention and recovery
support.text: Have all medicines checked, including seizure drugs, steroids, antibiotics, antifungals, non-prescription products and supplements. The team will confirm the local antifungal prevention plan and choose medicines that avoid vincristine interactions. Other infection prevention follows the individual specialist plan.

monitoring_summary: Before starting: Blood count, kidney/liver tests; hearing assessment and creatinine clearance when clinically indicated; NCCP lung testing for patients at high risk. Current lomustine SmPC additionally advises baseline lung-function assessment. Current cisplatin product information advises baseline audiometry. Confirm recovery after RT and the individual hydration/electrolyte plan. During treatment: Regular blood count, kidney/liver tests, with hearing and lung assessment when indicated. Current lomustine SmPC advises weekly blood counts for at least six weeks after a dose and continuing lung assessment. Current cisplatin product information additionally advises weekly kidney/liver tests, blood counts and electrolytes through treatment, with repeat hearing testing for symptoms. Review nerves and bowel function before vincristine. Brain/spine imaging and any other response tests follow the individual specialist plan; no universal scan or tumour-marker timetable is set here.

evidence.title: CLV evidence: adult context and paediatric origins
evidence.intro: The NCCP CLV regimen cites studies of cisplatin, lomustine and vincristine with radiotherapy in children with medulloblastoma.
evidence.population: The cited Packer 1994 study concerns children with medulloblastoma; this NCCP regimen is for selected adults.
evidence.interpretation: The treatment strategy has a role in specialist multimodal care, but paediatric outcomes cannot be used as an adult survival estimate or applied to every embryonal tumour.
limitations: The cited childhood study does not establish a numerical benefit for this exact adult high-risk population.
Medulloblastoma and other embryonal tumours have different molecular and clinical contexts. Glioma trials and the uploaded glioma guide do not establish CLV efficacy.
The neuro-oncology team must explain the evidence, uncertainties, treatment burden and alternatives for the individual diagnosis.

chapters.title: Your treatment and its purpose
chapters.intro: Keep the exact diagnosis, regimen and treatment goal together.

items.title: Why this treatment?
items.text: CLV combines three chemotherapy medicines after craniospinal radiotherapy for selected adults with high-risk medulloblastoma or another eligible embryonal tumour. It is part of a specialist treatment plan; it is not a glioma regimen.

items.title: What each medicine does
items.text: Lomustine: Lomustine is an oral nitrosourea chemotherapy that can reach the brain. It damages DNA and interferes with cell division. Its effects on healthy blood-forming cells can appear several weeks after the dose and can build up over successive cycles. This explains the long gap between doses and the need for continuing blood tests. Cisplatin: Cisplatin forms chemical links within DNA, making it harder for cells to copy and repair their genetic material. It can damage tumour cells but also affect kidney function, hearing, nerves and blood-forming cells. Fluids, electrolyte checks and anti-sickness medicines are part of the treatment plan to reduce avoidable harm. Vincristine: Vincristine interferes with structures that cells use when dividing. It can also affect nerves controlling sensation, strength and bowel movement. This explains why tingling, weakness and constipation need early review even if blood tests are satisfactory.

items.title: Your schedule
items.text: Start four to six weeks after craniospinal radiotherapy, once cleared by your team. In each 42-day cycle, lomustine is taken once on Day 1, cisplatin is infused on Day 1, and vincristine is infused on Days 1, 8 and 15. Eight cycles are planned, with individual safety review.

items.title: Evidence and uncertainty
items.text: The treatment strategy has a role in specialist multimodal care, but paediatric outcomes cannot be used as an adult survival estimate or applied to every embryonal tumour. The cited childhood study does not establish a numerical benefit for this exact adult high-risk population. Medulloblastoma and other embryonal tumours have different molecular and clinical contexts. Glioma trials and the uploaded glioma guide do not establish CLV efficacy. The neuro-oncology team must explain the evidence, uncertainties, treatment burden and alternatives for the individual diagnosis.

chapters.title: Understanding your particular brain tumour
chapters.intro: CLV here is for selected adult high-risk medulloblastoma or another eligible embryonal tumour; it is not a glioma regimen.

items.title: The exact diagnosis matters
items.text: Medulloblastoma is an embryonal tumour that usually starts in the cerebellum. The NCCP regimen also names other primitive neuro-ectodermal tumours, including pinealoblastoma. Ask the specialist to record the current pathology name and explain any older wording. These diagnoses are not interchangeable with glioblastoma or other gliomas.

items.title: Risk group and spread
items.text: The team considers the exact tumour, what remains after surgery and whether it has spread within the brain, spine or cerebrospinal fluid. Ask what makes your tumour high risk and which results establish that. A general glioma grade explanation does not replace medulloblastoma risk assessment.

items.title: Molecular results
items.text: Medulloblastoma can be classified by molecular findings, including WNT, SHH and non-WNT/non-SHH groups. Ask which tests apply to your exact tumour and how they affect discussion. Molecular tests used for another tumour type are not automatically relevant to this diagnosis. If a result is pending or not applicable, record that clearly.

items.title: How the treatments fit together
items.text: Surgery obtains tissue and removes tumour where safely possible. Craniospinal radiotherapy treats planned areas of the brain and spine. This NCCP CLV schedule starts four to six weeks after craniospinal RT, after recovery and safety review. The team confirms the role of each part for your diagnosis.

items.title: A useful diagnosis record
items.text: Keep the pathology date and wording, risk group and its reasons, molecular results if relevant, surgery and RT dates, brain/spine scan findings and any cerebrospinal-fluid assessment. Ask who will explain pending results. Use this record to understand decisions, not to determine your own chemotherapy eligibility.

chapters.title: Tests, scans and recovery after treatment
chapters.intro: Safety tests and tumour-response tests have different purposes.

items.title: Bloods, kidneys and hydration
items.text: Blood counts check marrow recovery; kidney and liver tests help assess whether treatment is safe. Cisplatin also needs an individual hydration and electrolyte plan. Tell staff about fluid restrictions, swelling, heart or kidney problems and difficulty drinking. Do not use a generic home fluid target in place of your plan. Current cisplatin product information advises weekly blood-count, kidney/liver and electrolyte checks through treatment.

items.title: Hearing, nerves and lung assessment
items.text: Cisplatin can affect hearing and nerves; vincristine can affect nerves and bowel function; lomustine can affect the lungs. Tell the team about changes before every visit. NCCP lists hearing and lung tests according to clinical need, while current lomustine product information advises baseline and continuing lung assessment. Ask which checks are booked for you. Current cisplatin product information advises a hearing test before treatment and repeat testing if hearing symptoms develop.

items.title: Brain and spine review
items.text: Medulloblastoma may involve the brain, spine or cerebrospinal fluid. Your specialist decides which imaging or other tests are needed at each stage. Keep the next scan date and result-review appointment in your passport. This guide does not set a universal scan, lumbar-puncture or blood tumour-marker timetable.

items.title: Delayed effects and rehabilitation
items.text: Symptoms may change after surgery, RT or chemotherapy. Hearing, balance, strength, memory, fatigue and daily function deserve follow-up as well as scans. Ask which longer-term checks and rehabilitation are relevant after your particular treatment. Report new changes promptly rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

items.title: Keep results with decisions
items.text: Record when a test is booked, completed and explained, and the next agreed step. A normal result from one test does not replace another medicine-safety check. The team authorises treatment after considering symptoms, current results and earlier side effects.

chapters.title: Brain symptoms, medicines and when to call
chapters.intro: Symptoms may reflect the tumour, swelling, treatment, another medicine or a separate illness.

items.title: Know your usual symptoms
items.text: Before treatment, note your usual walking, strength, speech, sight, memory, sleep and seizure pattern. Record new changes and their timing. A trusted person can help if you want them involved.

items.title: Urgent neurological changes
items.text: Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice, including on treatment rest days. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow the emergency instructions in any established seizure rescue plan.

items.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
items.text: Steroids may reduce swelling around a brain tumour. If needed, ask for a written dose, review date and reduction plan; do not stop suddenly or adjust the dose yourself. Report infection symptoms, marked thirst, weakness or troublesome sleep or mood changes.

items.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
items.text: Take prescribed seizure medicine on its own schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and how to manage a breakthrough seizure. Do not switch or stop it yourself. Anyone giving a rescue medicine needs the personal instructions and training.

items.title: Safety at home and outside
items.text: Discuss driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery with your team, taking account of symptoms and seizures. Individual medical and licensing advice is needed. Occupational therapy can help make daily routines safer.

chapters.title: Your overall treatment plan and choices
chapters.intro: Treatment should account for the tumour and the life you want to lead.

items.title: Understand the sequence
items.text: Place biopsy or surgery, radiotherapy, medicines and follow-up on one plan. Concurrent means treatments overlap; adjuvant means treatment follows the main treatment. A new phase can require different doses, tests and support medicines.

items.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
items.text: Ask what treatment can reasonably achieve for your tumour and which effects matter most to you. Discuss benefits, burdens, alternatives and the reasons for a pause or stop.

items.title: Put evidence in context
items.text: A study result applies to a particular group, diagnosis and schedule. Older studies may use different tumour names. Ask which evidence fits your plan; an average cannot forecast your response or lifespan.

items.title: Discuss options available to you
items.text: Ask about suitable trials, another specialist opinion and other treatment or symptom-care options. Your multidisciplinary team explains what is appropriate and available for you.

items.title: Make room for your priorities
items.text: Bring up thinking, independence, family time, work and the side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for time, written notes or a supporter if that helps you weigh the choices.

chapters.title: Living well, rehabilitation and support
chapters.intro: Practical and symptom support can begin alongside anticancer treatment.

items.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
items.text: Tell the team about changes in memory, language, attention, sight or planning. Rehabilitation can involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or psychology. Ask for practical help with routines and medicines.

items.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
items.text: Use your prescribed nausea and bowel plan and report problems early. Ask for dietitian help if intake or weight falls. Adapt movement to your balance and strength, and ask the team to assess fatigue that disrupts daily life.

items.title: Emotional support and carers
items.text: Tell the team about changes in mood, behaviour or coping. Patients and carers may each need psychological or practical support. Agree who can receive information and ask for help before caring becomes overwhelming.

items.title: Work, transport and finances
items.text: Tell the nurse or social worker about travel, employment, finances and caring responsibilities. Arrange practical help with medicines or appointments if symptoms make those tasks difficult.

items.title: Supportive care and future wishes
items.text: Supportive and palliative care can help manage symptoms while treatment continues. When you are ready, discuss future care preferences and whom you want involved. Ask your team to help document these wishes.

items.title: Information that works on paper
items.text: Keep the latest paper schedule, medicine list, results plan and emergency contacts together. The treatment card helps others identify your regimen. It supports, but does not replace, the prescription and emergency instructions.

questions.q: What is my exact diagnosis and how does this regimen fit?
questions.a: NCCP 00806: selected adults with high-risk medulloblastoma or another eligible primitive neuro-ectodermal tumour, including pinealoblastoma. Ask for the pathology, relevant molecular findings and the treatment goal in plain language.

questions.q: Which medicines do I receive on which days?
questions.a: Start four to six weeks after craniospinal radiotherapy, once cleared by your team. In each 42-day cycle, lomustine is taken once on Day 1, cisplatin is infused on Day 1, and vincristine is infused on Days 1, 8 and 15. Eight cycles are planned, with individual safety review.

questions.q: Which tests must happen before the next treatment?
questions.a: Before starting: Blood count, kidney/liver tests; hearing assessment and creatinine clearance when clinically indicated; NCCP lung testing for patients at high risk. Current lomustine SmPC additionally advises baseline lung-function assessment. Current cisplatin product information advises baseline audiometry. Confirm recovery after RT and the individual hydration/electrolyte plan. During treatment: Regular blood count, kidney/liver tests, with hearing and lung assessment when indicated. Current lomustine SmPC advises weekly blood counts for at least six weeks after a dose and continuing lung assessment. Current cisplatin product information additionally advises weekly kidney/liver tests, blood counts and electrolytes through treatment, with repeat hearing testing for symptoms. Review nerves and bowel function before vincristine. Brain/spine imaging and any other response tests follow the individual specialist plan; no universal scan or tumour-marker timetable is set here.

questions.q: How do I handle a missed, vomited or held dose?
questions.a: Contact the oncology team or pharmacist for medicine-specific instructions. Do not double a dose or replace treatment that was held for toxicity.

questions.q: Who helps with steroids, seizures, hearing, memory or daily tasks?
questions.a: Ask for written medicine plans and a named contact. Rehabilitation, practical support and a trusted helper may support the daily plan.

questions.q: Which symptoms mean I should call now?
questions.a: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Call promptly for fever, bleeding, new cough or breathlessness, persistent vomiting or reduced urine. Report hearing, nerve or bowel changes before the next infusion.

questions.q: When do we review whether treatment is helping?
questions.a: Agree the next clinical and imaging review, what would count as benefit, how side effects will be weighed and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping.
